messages.subject: Speed of a single iteration
parts:
Hi all

I'm trying to get my head around how a single interation in NUTS proceeds. From the paper it seems like the running time of a single iteration should be approximately

O([number of leapfrog steps] * [time to compute derivatives for a leapfrog step])

Is this the case? When sampler optimization is discussed here we usually focus on reparameterizations that make sampling "easier". Does the following mechanism explain why this works?

sampling easier -> fewer rejected proposals -> larger step size needed to achieve desired acceptance rate -> fewer leapfrog steps on average before u-turn -> faster iterations

Does this suggest that I could speed up sampling by reducing adapt_delta (as long as it didn't result in more than a few divergent transitions)?

Also, is vectorization the only way to decrease the derivative computation time?

Cheers
Sam

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Speed of a single iteration
parts:
> I'm trying to get my head around how a single interation in NUTS proceeds. From the paper it seems like the running time of a single iteration should be approximately
>
> O([number of leapfrog steps] * [time to compute derivatives for a leapfrog step])
>
> Is this the case?

> When sampler optimization is discussed here we usually focus on reparameterizations that make sampling "easier". Does the following mechanism explain why this works?
>
> sampling easier -> fewer rejected proposals -> larger step size needed to achieve desired acceptance rate -> fewer leapfrog steps on average before u-turn -> faster iterations

The causality is not quite correct. Better model implementations have two effects.

Firstly they can make the optimal integration time (epsilon * number of leapfrog steps)
decrease, which means fewer leapfrog steps regardless of epsilon.

Secondly, they can lead to larger epsilon. The step size has to match the
smallest length scale in the posterior, and better model implementations can
have larger smallest length scales.

Typically the integration time will scale with the longest length scale so the
number of leapfrog steps will scale as

number of leapfrog steps = integration time / step size \approx coefficient * longest length scale / shortest length scale.

Ideal posteriors have the same length scale in each parameter direction,
so that the ratio of length scales is unity, and decrease that leading
coefficient.
> Does this suggest that I could speed up sampling by reducing adapt_delta (as long as it didn't result in more than a few divergent transitions)?

Reducing from delta = 0.8 to anywhere above 0.6 may lead to marginally
faster execution, but below 0.6 is likely to be much worse. In general you
want to stick to the interval [0.6, 0.8] unless there are divergences, and
if there are divergences look to larger values to decrease the step size.
> Also, is vectorization the only way to decrease the derivative computation time?

You can also try to reuse shared expressions and avoid unnecessary
computation (such as inverting a constant matrix).

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Speed of a single iteration
parts:
> On Apr 5, 2016, at 9:58 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> ...

>> Also, is vectorization the only way to decrease the derivative computation time?
>
> You can also try to reuse shared expressions and avoid unnecessary
> computation (such as inverting a constant matrix).

As usual, the fastest code is no code (as in don't recompute something
if you don't have to).

You can also use compound expressions, such as multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(L)
instead of L * L'.

- Bob
